title_candidates: Claude's iPhone chat built a 3D game in three hours
Tree Appreciator is a small test of AI-made interaction
summary: Simon Willison prompted Claude's ordinary iPhone chat to make a 3D game. A no-account playtest checks the result's controls, rewards, persistence, and accessibility.

primary_source.title: Tree Appreciator
primary_source.author: Simon Willison
key_facts: Simon Willison asked Claude Opus 5.5 Max in the standard Claude iPhone app's chat mode—not Claude Code—to make a spot-the-difference game about two generated trees.
The prompt asked for a Three.js game that was both fun and visually appealing.
Claude worked for 3 hours and 7 minutes before returning a playable browser game.
The result includes generated tree pairs, synchronized rotation and zoom, music, animation, hints, achievements, scoring, and a saved herbarium of completed pairs.
The live game requires WebGL and offers touch, mouse, and keyboard controls, but its small visual differences may be difficult for some readers to see.

supporting_sources.title: Tree Appreciator
key_facts: The public game exposes the exact controls and feedback readers can test without an account.
Progress is stored in the current browser, and starting a new walk clears the herbarium and field-guide progress.

supporting_sources.title: Tree Appreciator build record
key_facts: The public build record links the original prompt, model, generated commit, and shared Claude transcript.
The finished game can therefore be compared with the short request that started it.

prerequisites: A current browser with WebGL enabled
No account, Claude subscription, coding, upload, or personal information
Ability to distinguish small visual differences; keyboard controls exist, but the game may still be difficult with low vision or color-vision limitations

steps.instruction: Open Tree Appreciator, confirm that two 3D trees load, read the tutorial, and select Got it. If a WebGL warning appears, try an updated supported browser; do not install an unfamiliar extension or weaken browser security.

Play the first pair without Hint: drag to rotate both trees, pinch or scroll to zoom, and select one visible difference. Confirm that the game marks it and advances the noticed counter; a miss should reduce the score slightly.

Find the remaining differences. If stuck for two minutes, select Hint once and observe how it guides you and changes the leaf rating. Finish the pair and confirm that a herbarium summary shows time and misses.
Select Next pair and complete three pairs to reach the Connoisseur's round. Answer its visual question and note whether the feedback makes the judgment understandable rather than merely surprising.

Open Field Guide, switch to Herbarium, and confirm completed pairs were saved. Reload the page and check that the entries remain. Do not select Start a new walk unless you intend to erase that progress.

Write a three-line verdict: one clear control, one moment that created attention or fun, and one friction or accessibility problem. Judge the finished interaction rather than the novelty of AI generating it.

risk_flags: The article describes one creator's experiment, not a general benchmark of Claude's reliability or game-design ability.
The game depends on WebGL and small visual differences, so not every device or reader can complete the exercise.
The guide evaluates a fixed public artifact and deliberately does not repeat Signal's August 6 browser-game creation workflow.
